item.title: 🟠 Engineer Overhead Lines to Withstand Ice, Wind and FreezingRain
item.description:
Why this matters: Service impact is possible — verify vendor status before troubleshooting internally.


This White Paper explains how ice, wind and vegetation load overhead distribution lines at the same time. It shows engineers how to assess the complete line and compare resilience options.

What you will learn about:

  • How freezing rain, rime ice and wet snow add weight to conductors and change their shape in the wind.
  • Why a moderate wind on a heavily iced line can govern design, and how galloping and vegetation contact create outages.
  • How a messenger-supported spacer cable separates the electrical function of covered conductors from the main mechanical load path.
  • How monitored severe-weather test data compares tension changes in bare, covered and spacer cable systems.
  • What utility records from the December 2008 Northeast ice storm show about circuit availability and restoration.
  • How to compare options at corridor level, check the full load path of poles, brackets and foundations, and apply energized-line safety rules.

item.title: 🟠 When Electric Cars Were for Women
item.description:
Why this matters: Could affect sign-ins, MFA, or Conditional Access — watch for authentication issues.


At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.

For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.
